content: 1. The emergency department (ED) staff, including doctors and nurses, should improve their utilization of the trauma team concept, ensuring a designated leader is present to coordinate care effectively. Record-keeping practices need enhancement to ensure accurate documentation of patient care. Targeted education should be provided, focusing on the management of patients in shock, including dedicated grand rounds sessions or other educational formats like journal clubs. These sessions should emphasize the appropriate management and optimal resuscitation of hemodynamically unstable patients. 2. A 50-year-old male construction worker fell from a height and experienced seizures at the scene. He was hemodynamically unstable during transport, with no vital signs recorded by paramedics. In the ED, his systolic blood pressure improved from 80 to 120 after fluid administration. His Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score was 7, and he was intubated 30 minutes after arrival following a respiratory arrest with seizures. A CT scan revealed a subdural hematoma, and he was treated with furosemide and mannitol before undergoing a craniotomy. Despite the intervention, he died in the ICU four hours later and was declared brain dead six hours after arrival. Autopsy findings included left femur and tibia fractures, as well as temporal and skull-base fractures. Deficiencies in care included inappropriate use of diuretics in a hypotensive patient, delays in work-up for hypotension, delayed intubation, and inadequate respiratory management in the presence of severe respiratory acidosis. Systemic issues included a lack of leadership in resuscitation efforts. Corrective actions include targeted education on airway management and resuscitation, improved respiratory management in the operating room (OR) and ICU, and the development of protocols for immediate intubation in patients with a GCS <8. 3. A 75-year-old male involved in a motor vehicle collision (MVC) was found in cardiac arrest at the prehospital scene. He underwent CPR, defibrillation, and bag-valve-mask ventilation before being intubated in the ED. He had bilateral above-knee amputations and died 15 minutes after ED arrival. Autopsy revealed no other injuries. Deficiencies included a lack of external hemorrhage control and fluid resuscitation. Prehospital and systemic inadequacies were noted, including the need for improved medical control of prehospital care. Corrective actions include enhanced communication between field and hospital, improved prehospital triage, and targeted education for prehospital providers on hemorrhage control techniques, including the use of direct pressure and tourniquets. 4. A 45-year-old male sustained blunt chest trauma in a motorcycle crash. He required intubation in the ED due to tachypnea. Imaging revealed multiple right rib fractures and a pneumothorax, which was treated with a chest tube. He was admitted to the ICU for mechanical ventilation and later weaned off after four days. He was stable and ready for transfer to the ward on face mask oxygen. However, his DVT prophylaxis (subcutaneous heparin) was not renewed during the transfer orders. He went two days without prophylaxis while bedridden, and heparin was restarted after the omission was noted. The patient became hypotensive and short of breath, requiring re-intubation and ICU transfer, but he died during the diagnostic work-up. Autopsy revealed a large pulmonary embolus. The omission of DVT prophylaxis during the transfer was a critical error.
